entries.verbatim: ## Questions fréquentes sur la vente des produits physiques sur systeme.io Comment vendre des produits physiques avec systeme.io ? Créez une fiche produit dans votre compte systeme.io depuis la section Produits. Ajoutez vos images, définissez le prix, configurez les variantes comme la taille ou la couleur, puis ajoutez vos frais de livraison. Ensuite, ajoutez le produit à une étape de tunnel ou à une page de site avec un bouton d’achat. Lorsqu’un client achète, il est redirigé vers la page de paiement. Le paiement est traité via Stripe ou PayPal, puis la commande apparaît dans votre tableau de bord pour être préparée et expédiée. Vous pouvez aussi ajouter des upsells et des séquences email après achat depuis la même plateforme.

Customers who have come from that setup describe it in their own words: a website on one side, email marketing on the other, and a third-party course creator they were trying to integrate; one says the thing she values is no longer juggling multiple tools; another says she was able to cancel several other apps and keep a single space for her business. The seams are where her week goes — the launch depends on a purchase in one tool producing access in another, and she is the integration. Any figures for what the stack costs her or how long the handoffs take are not documented here, only that more than one customer framed the before-state as self-inflicted complication.

segments.name: A creator who sells a printed book and a small merch run to the same list that already buys her digital course
segments.situation: Her income is digital — a course, a few downloads, an email list she sells to directly. Then a physical item appears: a printed book, a small batch of merch, a workbook. The vendor positions exactly this person: businesses selling a limited range of physical products through funnels, creators selling merchandise, physical books or a small range of products alongside digital products. The conventional answer is a separate store subscription plus the work of wiring it to the funnel and list that already do the selling, and the vendor's own comparison prices that alternative at $39/month plus 2% on third-party processors, or self-hosting with plugin maintenance. Whether she actually balks at that is not documented here; what is documented is that the vendor built and aimed the feature at her, and openly says it is not for a large catalogue.

segments.name: A freelance marketing consultant running funnels and email for five client businesses out of one login
segments.situation: Each client needs their own pages, their own list and their own sequences, and keeping them apart matters more than any single feature. The vendor states sub-accounts are designed for agencies and consultants managing multiple clients, with each sub-account a fully independent space with its own funnels, contacts, emails and courses, unlimited on every plan and carrying the main plan's limits at no extra charge. Whether consultants are actually blocked today by per-client pricing or by mixing clients in one account is not documented in this material; the vendor's framing and the comparison targets it names — GoHighLevel, WordPress Multisite — are all we have.

objections.objection: "Everything bundled means everything is second-rate. My email tool, my course platform and my page builder are each better than one platform's version of them, and I will be downgrading five things to simplify one."
objections.answer: Partly answerable, and the honest version is stronger than the sales version. The vendor states every feature is available on every plan including free, with paid plans only raising limits (E66), and that 99% of features are accessible without limits (E125) — so the reader can test the real thing before deciding whether it is a downgrade. The vendor also concedes a real trade-off in writing: it is not designed for large e-commerce with advanced catalogue management or complex logistics (E22), and it says Shopify and WooCommerce offer much more advanced inventory and logistics tools for primarily physical businesses (E21). One buyer who ran this comparison himself concluded systeme.io had just as much to offer as Kajabi at very affordable rates (E113) — that is his assessment, not verified parity. Nothing in the evidence compares deliverability, editor depth or course features feature-by-feature against the incumbents.

objections.objection: "Moving is the whole problem. My list, my live course with students mid-cohort, my domain and my paid traffic all point at the current setup. A weekend of migration I do not have, and if I break a checkout I lose real sales."
objections.answer: Partly. The free plan with no credit card lets the whole thing be built and tested in parallel before switching anything (E147, E30, E78), which removes the all-at-once risk. Free migration is offered (E77), and the migration team will help — but only after signing up for the Illimité plan or an annual plan (E18), so the help is conditional on paying. The vendor is explicit that there is no automatic product import yet and product listings must be recreated manually (E17). No evidence here covers migrating an existing course with enrolled students, preserving email history or redirecting live ad traffic, and no refund or reversal guarantee exists in this material.

objections.objection: "What does it actually cost once I pass 2,000 contacts? €0 is the hook; I need the number for year two before I move my business onto it."
objections.answer: Not answerable with what we have, and this is the largest hole in the evidence. The named paid plans and their prices are not legible in the retrieved pricing content. All we can say is the shape: free entry at €0 (E28), 2,000 contacts, unlimited emails and a first funnel on the free plan (E30), paid plans differ only by raising limits rather than unlocking features (E66), and annual billing gives 2 free months (E76). Any specific paid price, tier name or contact ceiling must not be stated in copy — we do not have it.

objections.objection: "Unlimited emails on a free plan sounds like a spam farm. If my open rates drop or my domain gets burned because I share sending infrastructure with 500,000 free accounts, the cheap tool costs me the list."
objections.answer: Nothing in the evidence answers this. There is no deliverability data, no sending-domain or authentication detail, no inbox-placement figure and no statement about how free accounts are policed. Unlimited sending on all plans (E70, E34) is the only related fact, and it is the thing the objection is worried about, not the answer to it. Copy should not reassure on deliverability.

objections.objection: "If my site, list, courses, checkout and automations all live in one account, that company owns my business. One price rise, one outage, one policy change and I have no fallback."
objections.answer: Nothing in the evidence answers this. No uptime commitment, no SLA, no data-export or portability statement, no contract terms, and the offer summary records no guarantees. The nearest related facts cut the other way: consolidation is the product (E65, E143), and the vendor's own migration page shows how manual leaving a platform can be (E17). Support availability (E150, E75) answers responsiveness, not dependency.

objections.objection: "I have never heard of them. The proof is first names, five-star image captions and a round 500,000 figure the company counted itself."
objections.answer: Weakly, and the weakness should be respected rather than papered over. The user figures are self-reported with no date or methodology (E117, E29, E131, E127). The strongest named proof is thin: first-name customers describing consolidation and ease (E120, E121, E134, E135), and one buyer's own comparison against AWeber and Kajabi (E113). Two further five-star items are image captions, not testimonial text, with no customer named (E25, E26). Operationally there is a self-reported support response time under 2 hours, 7 days a week (E69, E150). There is no third-party audit, no named company case study and no dated result anywhere in the evidence.

objections.objection: "Bad timing. I just paid twelve months upfront on my funnel tool and I am mid-launch. Ask me in a year."
objections.answer: Yes. The free plan requires no credit card and includes 2,000 contacts, unlimited emails and the first funnel (E30, E78, E119), and the vendor states the free plan exists precisely to let you build and test everything before moving to a paid plan (E147) — so the next funnel can be built here at zero cost while the paid year runs out. When the switch does come, annual billing carries 2 free months plus free migration (E76, E77). Nothing in the evidence offers credit or compensation for an unused incumbent subscription.

objections.objection: "It will not hold my product range. The moment I have more than a handful of SKUs, real inventory or a 3PL, I am migrating again — and migrating a store is worse than migrating a list."
objections.answer: Honestly, and only for the small-range case. The vendor states plainly that it is not designed for large e-commerce needing advanced catalogue management, complex logistics integrations or very advanced inventory tools (E22), and that Shopify and WooCommerce are better for primarily physical businesses (E21). Within a limited range it is specific: variants with automatic SKU generation (E3), real-time stock tracking to avoid overselling (E4), shipping zones, carrier rates and rules by weight, order value or location (E6, E7), order filtering by date, status or product (E9), Stripe/PayPal payment then fulfilment from the dashboard (E10), and 0% transaction fees on all plans (E1). If the reader's catalogue is already large, the copy should disqualify them rather than win them.

objections.objection: "My clients cannot see another vendor's branding. If each client sits in a sub-account on my platform account, it looks like I resell someone else's software — and I lose the relationship when they log in."
objections.answer: Partly. Every plan allows unlimited sub-accounts, each a separate account with its own limits, at the main plan's limits and no extra charge (E67, E68), and each is a fully independent space with its own funnels, contacts, emails and courses (E51). White label goes further: your own custom domain, a fully branded client space, 100% of revenue and no transaction fees (E63). Assistant accounts also exist (E105). The gap: the evidence does not state which plans include white label or what it costs, and plan-specific availability is explicitly unstated for many features — so copy must not promise white label at a price.

objections.objection: "I could build this myself. WordPress plus a few plugins and a Zapier connection costs less and I keep control."
objections.answer: Reasonably. On the self-build side the vendor's comparison claims WooCommerce requires hosting, plugin maintenance and additional marketing tools (E20) — that is the vendor's claim about a rival, not independent verification. On its own side: a full site with multiple pages, blog and custom domain with no hosting, plugins or technical setup, included even on the free plan (E37), a site in under 10 minutes from templates (E31), and triggers/conditions/actions automation that connects purchase, course enrolment, email and CRM without Zapier or any external tool (E45, E143, E144).

objections.objection: "If it is this cheap, who answers me at 9pm the night of a launch when checkout breaks?"
objections.answer: Yes, on the vendor's own word. Support is available 7 days a week on all plans (E75), with a self-reported average response time under 2 hours and a stated caveat that it varies with request volume (E69, E150), email support listed as 24/7 (E107), a 1-on-1 onboarding coaching session (E106) and step-by-step video tutorials for every feature in the help centre (E148). All of it is self-reported and none of it is a contractual response-time commitment.
